tagline: Moses' farewell sermons on the plains of Moab: the covenant restated for a new generation, calling Israel to love the one God with the whole heart before it enters the land.
overview:
Deuteronomy is the last of the five books of the Torah (the Pentateuch, the Law of Moses), and it is mostly speech. Israel is camped on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan River and across from Jericho, at the end of forty years in the wilderness. The generation that left Egypt has died, and Moses, who will not be allowed to enter the land, gathers their children and preaches to them. He retells what God has done, restates the law given at Mount Sinai (which Deuteronomy usually calls Horeb), applies it to life in a settled country, and presses the people to choose between life and death. The English title comes from the Greek translation of the Old Testament called the Septuagint, which rendered a phrase in 17:18 as a second law, or a repetition of the law. The Hebrew title, Devarim, simply means words, taken from the book's opening line.

The book is built around three addresses by Moses. The first (chapters 1 to 4) reviews the road from Horeb to Moab and draws its lessons. The second and longest (chapters 5 to 28) repeats the Ten Commandments, calls Israel to love the LORD alone, and then sets out the statutes for worship, government, justice, family, and care for the poor, ending in blessings and curses. The third (chapters 29 and 30) renews the covenant with this new generation. The closing chapters hand leadership to Joshua, record a long song and a final blessing from Moses, and tell of his death on Mount Nebo, looking at a land he would not enter.

Deuteronomy has shaped Jewish and Christian faith as much as any book in the Old Testament. Its call in 6:4-5, known by its first Hebrew word as the Shema, became Israel's daily confession, and Jesus named it the greatest commandment. When Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, every answer he gave Satan came from Deuteronomy. The prophets preached its covenant, and the historical books from Joshua to Kings measure Israel's kings by its standard. It is a book about the heart: about loving God with the whole self, remembering what he has done, and refusing to forget him once life becomes comfortable.
author:
The book presents itself as the words of Moses, spoken on the plains of Moab and then written down by him (31:9, 31:24), and Jewish and Christian tradition has long held Moses to be its author. Jesus and the New Testament writers cite its commands as the words of Moses. The book also contains material Moses could not have written himself: the narrator's introduction (1:1-5), which calls the land east of the Jordan the land beyond the Jordan, a phrase many read as the standpoint of someone west of it (though Deuteronomy also uses it of the western side, as in 3:25), and the account of his death and burial in chapter 34. Jewish tradition in the Talmud assigned those final verses to Joshua, and traditional scholars generally see the book's substance as Mosaic with some later editorial framing.

Most critical scholars date the book, or its core in chapters 12 to 26, much later. In 1805 the German scholar W. M. L. de Wette argued that the scroll found in the temple during King Josiah's reign (2 Kings 22) was an early form of Deuteronomy, and this became the dominant view. On that reading the book grew from circles concerned with covenant faithfulness, perhaps with roots among Levites or prophets of the northern kingdom, was brought to Jerusalem, and was expanded during and after the Babylonian exile. Many scholars also see Deuteronomy as the theological opening of a larger history running from Joshua through Kings, a theory associated with Martin Noth in the mid-twentieth century. Conservative scholars reply that the book's form resembles treaties from the second millennium BC and that its setting before the conquest is consistent throughout.
date:
If Moses is the author, the book belongs to the end of the wilderness period, dated in the fifteenth century BC by those who hold an early date for the exodus (based on 1 Kings 6:1) or in the thirteenth century BC by those who hold a later one. The book itself dates Moses' speeches to the first day of the eleventh month of the fortieth year after the exodus (1:3).

Most critical scholars place the book's core in the seventh century BC, connecting it with Josiah's reform around 622 BC, when a book of the law was found in the temple and the king abolished worship outside Jerusalem (2 Kings 22 and 23). Deuteronomy's insistence on one central place of worship (chapter 12) matches that reform closely. Supporters of this view often point to parallels between the curses of chapter 28 and the treaty that the Assyrian king Esarhaddon imposed on his vassals in 672 BC. Supporters of an earlier date point instead to the overall shape of the book (history, stipulations, blessings and curses, witnesses, provision for public reading), which resembles Hittite vassal treaties of the late second millennium BC. Some scholars take a middle position: old Mosaic material, preserved and preached over centuries, and given its final form later.
setting:
The book's own setting is the plains of Moab, the lowland on the east side of the Jordan across from Jericho, just north of the Dead Sea. Israel has defeated Sihon, king of the Amorites at Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, and holds the land east of the Jordan, which Moses has given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh. Across the river lies Canaan, a land of walled city-states with their own kings and gods, among them Baal, the storm god, and Asherah, a mother goddess, whose worship Deuteronomy repeatedly warns against. Egypt to the southwest and the powers of Mesopotamia to the northeast are distant for now, but the whole region knew the form of a treaty between a great king and his vassals, and Deuteronomy uses that form to describe the relationship between the LORD and Israel.

The first readers heard the book as a word for a people at a threshold. Everything the land would offer (wells they did not dig, houses they did not build, abundance after scarcity) would tempt them to forget the God who gave it. If the book reached its final form later, as many scholars think, its readers also stood at a threshold of another kind, facing Assyrian pressure or Babylonian exile, and the book's warnings and its promise of return after exile (30:1-10) spoke directly to them.
purpose: Deuteronomy was given to renew the covenant with a generation that had not stood at Sinai, so that they would enter the land as God's people rather than as one more nation. It explains the law, not only restates it: Moses gives reasons, appeals to memory, and presses on motive. It aims at the heart, calling Israel to love, fear, serve, and cling to the LORD. It sets up institutions for life after Moses (judges, a king under the law, priests, and prophets) and makes provision for the law to be written, read aloud every seven years, and taught to children at home. It is preaching meant to be repeated, a pattern for how every later generation should hear God's word as addressed to them today.
story: Deuteronomy closes the Torah. Genesis tells of creation and the promise to Abraham of land, descendants, and blessing; Exodus of rescue from Egypt and the covenant at Sinai; Leviticus of how a holy God can live among a sinful people; and Numbers of the wilderness years, where the first generation refused to enter the land and died in the desert. Deuteronomy stands at the edge of the promise, with the land in sight and the lawgiver about to die. Joshua picks up the story immediately, with Israel crossing the Jordan under Moses' successor. The books that follow (Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings) read Israel's history through Deuteronomy's lens: faithfulness brings life in the land, and persistent idolatry brings the covenant curses, ending finally in exile. Deuteronomy's promise that God will gather his scattered people and circumcise their hearts looks beyond that exile to restoration.
christ: Deuteronomy runs through the life of Jesus. Tempted in the wilderness for forty days, as Israel was tested for forty years, he answered each temptation from this book: “Man shall not live on bread alone” (Matthew 4:4, from Deuteronomy 8:3), “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (Matthew 4:7, from 6:16), and “Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only” (Matthew 4:10, from 6:13). Where Israel failed its test, he kept faith. Asked for the greatest commandment, he quoted the Shema (Mark 12:29-30). Moses promised that “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers” (18:15), and Peter applied that promise to Jesus (Acts 3:22). Paul read the curse on anyone hanged on a tree (21:23) as the curse Christ bore for us (Galatians 3:13), and he found the nearness of God's word (30:14) fulfilled in the message of faith (Romans 10:6-8). The book's deepest longing, that God would circumcise his people's hearts so they could love him (30:6), is what the New Testament says God does through Christ and the Spirit.
reading: Read Deuteronomy as preaching, not as a legal code. Moses speaks in the second person, repeats himself for emphasis, and constantly says today, pulling each generation into the moment of decision. The laws in chapters 12 to 26 are often explained with reasons (because you were slaves in Egypt, so that the poor will not cry out against you), and those reasons are as important as the rules. Watch the key verbs: hear, remember, do not forget, love, fear, keep, and choose. Two common misreadings are worth avoiding. One treats the book as legalism, as if Israel earned God's favor by obedience, but Deuteronomy insists that God chose Israel out of love before they obeyed anything (7:7-8, 9:4-6). The other skips its hard passages, especially the commands to destroy the Canaanites; these need to be read honestly, in the light of the whole Bible, rather than ignored.

structure.title: Moses' first address: remembering the road
structure.summary: Moses reviews the forty years from Horeb to Moab, the failure at Kadesh, the victories east of the Jordan, and calls Israel to keep the law and never make an image of God.

structure.title: The heart of the covenant
structure.summary: The Ten Commandments are repeated, followed by the Shema and extended preaching on loving God alone, remembering his grace, and refusing both pride and idolatry.

structure.title: The statutes and ordinances
structure.summary: Laws for life in the land: one place of worship, the rejection of Canaanite religion, festivals, judges, kings, priests, prophets, warfare, family, and generous care for the poor, the widow, the orphan, and the foreigner.

structure.title: Blessings and curses
structure.summary: Instructions for a covenant ceremony at Mounts Ebal and Gerizim, followed by the blessings that come with obedience and the long list of curses, ending in exile, that come with rebellion.

structure.title: The covenant renewed in Moab
structure.summary: Moses renews the covenant with the new generation, foresees exile and return, promises that God will circumcise their hearts, and sets before them life and death.

structure.title: Moses' last words and death
structure.summary: Joshua is commissioned, the law is written and entrusted to the priests, Moses sings a song of witness and blesses the tribes, and he dies on Mount Nebo in sight of the land.

themes.title: One God, loved with the whole heart
themes.body: The center of Deuteronomy is the Shema: the LORD is one, and Israel must love him with all its heart, soul, and strength (6:4-5). The book's demand for exclusive loyalty flows from this. The LORD is not one god among many to be served alongside Baal or Asherah; he alone rescued Israel and he alone is to be worshiped. Love here is not only a feeling but covenant loyalty expressed in obedience, and it is commanded because it is owed to the God who loved first.

themes.title: Covenant and grace
themes.body: Deuteronomy is shaped like an ancient treaty between a great king and a vassal people, with history, obligations, blessings, curses, and witnesses. But the relationship begins with grace. Israel was not chosen because it was large or righteous (7:7-8, 9:4-6); God set his love on them and kept the oath he swore to their fathers. Obedience is the response to that grace, and the law is given for Israel's good, as the way to life in the land.

themes.title: Remember and do not forget
themes.body: Memory is one of the book's great concerns. Israel must remember that it was a slave in Egypt, that God led it through the wilderness, and that he fed it with manna. The great danger is not hardship but prosperity: when they have eaten and are satisfied in houses they did not build, they will be tempted to forget the LORD and credit themselves (8:11-18). Teaching children, reciting the law, and keeping the festivals all serve this memory.

themes.title: Justice for the vulnerable
themes.body: Deuteronomy's laws show striking concern for people with no power of their own: the widow, the orphan, the foreigner living in Israel, the Levite without land, the poor debtor, the hired worker, and the escaped slave. Debts are released every seventh year, gleanings are left in the fields, wages are paid the same day, and judges must not take bribes. The motive is repeatedly Israel's own history: remember that you were a slave in Egypt.

themes.title: The land as gift and test
themes.body: The land is God's gift, sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, a good land flowing with milk and honey. But it is held on covenant terms. Faithfulness means long life in it; idolatry means being driven from it. The book foresees exile and also return, promising that God will gather his scattered people and change their hearts (30:1-10), which gave hope to Israel in its darkest centuries.

keyChapters.why: Moses retells the failure at Kadesh-barnea, setting the tone for the whole book: the new generation must not repeat its parents' unbelief.
Moses warns against making any image of God, since Israel saw no form at Horeb, and foresees exile and return for a people who seek him with all their heart.
The Shema: the LORD is one, and Israel must love him with all its heart, soul, and strength, and teach these words to its children.
The wilderness as God's school, where Israel learned that man does not live on bread alone, and the warning against forgetting God in prosperity.
The law of the one place God will choose for worship, which shaped Israel's religion and later reforms.
The promise of a prophet like Moses, which the New Testament applies to Jesus.
The promise of return after exile and of hearts circumcised by God, and the call to choose life.
Moses dies on Mount Nebo in sight of the land, and the Torah closes by saying no prophet like him has yet arisen.
